texto:
Understanding the USD/JPY exchange rate requires close attention to interest rate differentials, particularly at the short end of the yield curve. The spread between US and Japanese 2-year government bond yields has consistently shown strong explanatory power for movements in the currency pair.

When the US 2-year yield rises relative to the Japanese equivalent, the interest rate differential widens. This dynamic increases the attractiveness of USD-denominated assets, leading to capital inflows into the United States and upward pressure on the USD/JPY exchange rate. Conversely, when the spread compresses, the incentive to hold dollar assets weakens, often resulting in USD depreciation against the yen.

This relationship is closely tied to the mechanics of the carry trade. Japan, characterized for decades by structurally low interest rates, has served as a funding currency. Investors borrow in yen at low cost and allocate capital into higher-yielding assets abroad, particularly in US fixed income markets. The profitability of this strategy depends directly on the stability and magnitude of the yield differential.

During periods of aggressive monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve combined with accommodative policy from the Bank of Japan, the carry trade becomes especially attractive. The widening spread amplifies capital flows into US assets and reinforces USD strength. However, the strategy is highly sensitive to changes in global liquidity conditions, volatility, and shifts in monetary policy expectations. Any signal of normalization in Japanese rates or easing in US rates can trigger rapid unwinding of positions, leading to sharp currency adjustments.

From a macro-financial perspective, the USD/JPY pair can therefore be interpreted as a market-based proxy for interest rate divergence and cross-border capital allocation. Monitoring short-term yield spreads remains essential for anticipating directional moves in the exchange rate and assessing the sustainability of carry-driven positioning.
